title: The Story of the Young King of the Black Isles
paragraphs: Sire, you should know that my father was Mahmoud, king of this country, the Black Isles. It is called that because of the four small mountains that were once islands, and where the great lake now lies there used to be the capital. My story will explain how all this came about.
My father died at the age of sixty-six, and I took his throne. I married my cousin, whom I loved dearly, and I believed she loved me in return.

But one afternoon, as I lay half asleep while two of her maids fanned me, I heard one of them say to the other, “What a shame that our mistress doesn’t love our master anymore! I think she’d kill him if she could, since she’s an enchantress.”

I watched her and soon saw that the maids were right. Then I gave one of her favorite slaves a mortal wound for a terrible crime, and she asked me to let her build a palace in the garden, where she mourned and wept for him for two years.

In the end I begged her to stop grieving. He could neither speak nor move, I told her, and only her enchantments kept him alive. She turned on me in fury and spoke some magic words over me, and in that instant I became what you see now: half man, half marble.

Then this wicked enchantress turned the capital, a populous and thriving city, into the lake and the barren plain you crossed. The fish of four colors in the lake are the different peoples who lived in the city, and the four hills are the four islands that give my kingdom its name. She told me all this just to add to my misery. And that is not all. Every day she comes and lashes me with a whip of buffalo hide.
When the young king had finished his sad story, he burst into tears again, and the Sultan was deeply moved.
“Tell me,” the Sultan cried, “where is this wicked woman, and where is the wretched creature she loves, the one she barely keeps alive?”
“I don’t know where she lives,” the unhappy prince answered, “but every day at sunrise, after she has beaten me, she goes to see whether the slave can speak to her yet.”
“Unfortunate king,” said the Sultan, “I will do whatever I can to avenge you.”

He and the young king talked over the best way to do it, and they agreed to carry out their plan the following day. The Sultan then rested, and the young king let himself hope for freedom. The next day the Sultan rose and went to the palace in the garden where the black slave lay. He drew his sword and finished off the little life left in him, then threw the body down a well. After that he lay down on the couch where the slave had been and waited for the enchantress.
She went first to the young king and gave him a hundred lashes.
Then she came to the room where she believed her wounded slave was lying, though it was the Sultan on the couch.
She approached the couch and said, “Are you feeling better today, my dear slave? Say just one word to me.”
“How could I feel better,” the Sultan answered, mimicking the speech of the Ethiopians, “when your husband’s cries and groans never let me sleep?”
“What joy to hear you speak!” the queen replied. “Do you want him to have his own shape back?”
“Yes,” said the Sultan. “Hurry and set him free, so I don’t have to hear his cries any longer.”

The queen went out at once, took a cup of water, and spoke some words over it that made it boil as though it stood on a fire. Then she threw it over the prince, who immediately took back his own form. He was overjoyed, but the enchantress said, “Get away from here and never return, or I’ll kill you.”
So he hid, to watch how the Sultan’s plan would end.
Back at the Palace of Tears, the enchantress announced, “It is done, just as you wanted.”

“What you have done,” said the Sultan, “is not enough to heal me. Every night at midnight, all the people you turned into fish raise their heads out of the lake and cry out for vengeance. Go quickly and give them back their proper shapes.”
The enchantress rushed off and spoke some words over the lake.

The fish turned into men, women and children, and the houses and shops filled up again. The Sultan’s attendants, who had camped beside the lake, were astounded to find themselves in the middle of a large and beautiful city.
As soon as she had broken the spell on the city, the queen returned to the palace.
“Are you completely well now?” she asked.
“Come closer,” said the Sultan. “Closer still.”
She did as he said. Then he leapt up and, with a single stroke of his sword, cut her in half.
Then he went to find the prince.
“Rejoice,” he said. “Your cruel enemy is dead.”
The prince thanked him over and over.
“And now,” said the Sultan, “I will go back to my capital, which I’m glad to find is so close to yours.”
“So close to mine!” said the King of the Black Isles.
“Don’t you know it is a full year’s journey from here? You got here in a few hours only because the land was enchanted. But I will go with you on your way.”
“I would be very glad of your company,” said the Sultan, “and since I have no children, I will make you my heir.”
Together the Sultan and the prince started out, the Sultan carrying costly presents given him by the King of the Black Isles.
The day after he reached his capital, the Sultan called his court together and told them everything that had happened to him, and that he meant to adopt the young king as his heir.
Then he gave every man a present suited to his rank.
As for the fisherman, who had been the first cause of the young prince’s rescue, the Sultan gave him a large sum of money and made him and his family prosperous for the rest of their lives.
